quotes.section_title: Where does the quality gain come from?

quotes.text: Unguided delegation already cuts the lead’s cost by 29% and gains 5.3 points; partial routing adds 2.9 points to this for $0.08 more per build.

claims.text: Partial routing profiles solo traces of the lead and worker models: an LLM annotator labels recurring subtasks, and an LLM judge scores each model on each subtask, producing delegation tiers without training any model.
On held-out ViBench at delta=0.75, partial routing scores higher than the lead alone at lower cost, and it beats both the task-level routers and unguided delegation.
On held-out Terminal-Bench at delta=0.75, partial routing has the highest pass rate of any method, at about the lead's cost.
Giving the lead only the subtask plan, with no worker, cuts cost on both benchmarks at a similar or higher score.
The judge's quality scores and the tiers stay stable across repeated judge runs.
Profiling is cheap relative to training an orchestrator.
With a second model pair, partial routing improved the Terminal-Bench pass rate at lower cost. On ViBench it traded some score for a large cost reduction.
A low delta can underperform the lead alone on ViBench, so the choice of delta matters.

limits_authors.text: The main results use one model pair per benchmark and a small number of held-out tasks and runs.
It is untested whether the gains hold for model pairs with smaller capability or price gaps.
The sensitivity to rho, tau and the number of profiling tasks was not studied.
The annotator's labels and the judge's scores were not validated against human labels.
The authors did not check whether the lead actually followed its assigned tiers.

likely_overclaims: The abstract's Terminal-Bench gain rests on a small held-out set run twice, with no significance testing. The difference amounts to only a few task outcomes.
The authors say the second-pair runs indicate the gains carry over. But they are single runs without baselines, and on ViBench partial routing scored below the lead alone.
The paper's comparison table calls the method uniquely dynamic, informed and controllable. That rests on the authors' own qualitative categorization of related work.
Attributing the worker gains to context management is a hypothesis that no experiment tests.
Results at low delta underperform the lead alone on ViBench. This weakens the framing that delta is a smooth cost–quality control.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Partial routing. Offline, the lead and the worker each do the same tasks alone, and an LLM annotator then tags each step of their rollouts (gray) with a recurring subtask from a set \mathcal{S}; an LLM judge scores both models on each subtask, and \delta turns quality and cost saving into delegation tiers. Online, the lead follows this policy and briefs a fresh worker whenever it hands off a subtask. The five subtasks, their scores and their tiers at \delta=0.40 are from Table 2.

Figure 2: Cost and quality on the ten held-out ViBench applications, mean of three runs. The oracle curve sweeps \theta with hindsight (marked point: \theta=100, as in Table 3); the dashed line is the Pareto frontier of methods without hindsight. Higher scores and lower costs are better.

Figure 3: Cost and pass rate on the 23 held-out Terminal-Bench tasks, mean of two runs per task. Both axes are broken to fit GPT-6 Luna alone. Markers, labels and the dashed frontier are as in Figure 2.

change_for_agents: Instead of training an orchestrator, agent builders can profile logged solo traces into per-subtask delegate/conditional/keep tiers and put them in the lead's prompt, then tune delta on a validation set. Even a subtask plan alone, without a worker, can cut cost.

compact.claim: Guiding a frontier lead to delegate profiled subtasks to a cheaper worker beats both solo models and task-level routing on cost–quality, without training any model.
compact.method: An LLM annotator labels recurring subtasks in solo traces of the lead and worker, and an LLM judge scores each model per subtask. Savings and risk are combined with a parameter delta into delegate/conditional/keep tiers that go in the lead's prompt.

results.finding: On ViBench at delta=0.75, the score rises from 70.2 to 78.5 at 19% lower cost.
On Terminal-Bench at delta=0.75, the pass rate is 60.9% against 54.3% for the lead alone and for unguided delegation.
The plan alone cuts the lead's cost by 39% on ViBench and 16% on Terminal-Bench.
Across four judge re-runs, quality scores vary by at most 0.3 points.

compact.limits: Results come from one model pair per benchmark with few held-out tasks and runs, and the LLM judge was not validated against human labels.
